summary: An Internet Architecture Board memo describing the standardization state of Internet protocols at the time. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 2000, one of a regular series of such lists.

eli5.summary: Like a report card for all the network rules, showing which ones were official and which were still being tested. This one is old and was replaced by a newer list.

questions: what is the list of internet official protocol standards
where to find protocol standardization status
what are the protocol maturity levels
how does a protocol become a standard
what is the difference between draft standard and proposed standard
subtitle: The Internet Architecture Board's inventory of protocol standardization status.

tldr.problem: The Internet community needs a way to track which protocols are official standards, which are experimental, and which are no longer current.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1920 documents the standardization process, explains the different maturity levels (proposed, draft, standard) and status categories (required, recommended, elective), and provides lists of protocols in each category.
tldr.outcome: This experimental document served as a snapshot of protocol standards in March 1996. It was superseded by RFC 2000 as part of the regular quarterly updates to the standards inventory.

today: RFC 1920 is a Historic document and has been obsoleted by RFC 2000. It was part of a regular series of protocol standards snapshots intended to be updated quarterly. For the current standardization process and status of protocols, consult the RFC Editor's site and the current version of the Internet Official Protocol Standards.

sections.title: Overview of Standardization
sections.content: RFC 1920 describes the standardization process for Internet protocols as maintained by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB). The RFC explains the two independent ways protocols are categorized: their maturity level (state of standardization) and their requirement level (status or necessity). The document provides lists of all Internet protocols grouped by their maturity level and discusses the procedures the RFC Editor and IESG use to make standardization decisions.
sections.eli5: The RFC explains how new network rules get tested and approved to become official Internet standards, and keeps a big list showing which rules are official and which are still experimental.

sections.title: Maturity Levels
sections.content:
Protocols progress through five maturity levels. Standard protocols are official and assigned STD numbers by the IESG. Draft Standard protocols are under active IESG consideration with substantial testing underway. Proposed Standard protocols are candidates that may be considered for standardization in the future. Experimental protocols are for research, and implementers should coordinate with the developers. Historic protocols are superseded or no longer used.

A protocol typically starts at proposed standard (requiring at least 6 months before advancement to draft standard), then draft standard (requiring at least 4 months before advancement to standard). Proposals to draft standard require at least two independent implementations; proposals to standard require operational experience and demonstrated interoperability. In cases of uncertainty, a special review committee may be appointed.
sections.eli5: New rules start as suggestions, get tested, and if they work well, become official. Experimental ones are for testing. Old rules that do not work anymore become 'historic.'

sections.title: Requirement Levels (Status)
sections.content:
In addition to maturity level, each protocol has a requirement level that indicates how widely it should be implemented. Required protocols must be implemented in all systems. Recommended protocols should be implemented. Elective protocols may or may not be implemented, but if chosen, must be done exactly as specified. Limited Use protocols apply only in specific circumstances. Not Recommended protocols are discouraged for general use.

The RFC notes that few protocols are universally required, because systems vary widely (gateways, routers, workstations, hosts, etc.). Detailed applicability statements and separate requirements documents may provide more specific guidance for particular protocol implementations.
sections.eli5: Each rule gets labeled for what systems should use it: some are required for everything, some are recommended, and some are only for special cases.

sections.title: The Standards Track Process
sections.content:
The RFC defines the standards track as the progression path for protocols becoming Internet standards. A protocol enters the track only by IESG recommendation at the proposed standard level. The track includes a detailed decision table showing how the RFC Editor processes submissions based on source (IAB, IESG, IRTF, or other) and desired status.

The RFC includes a standards track diagram showing how protocols flow through the states. A protocol may move between proposed, draft, and standard states only by IESG action. Protocols may also branch off to experimental state if they are not ready for standardization, or become historic when superseded. Single-line boxes represent temporary states (expected to last several months), while double-line boxes represent long-term states.
sections.eli5: There is a specific path rules follow: first you propose it, then people test it for months, then if it works, it becomes official. Sometimes a rule stays experimental or becomes 'historic' if people do not need it.

sections.title: RFC Publication and Status
sections.content:
The RFC explains that RFCs are the working notes of the Internet research and development community, and range from meeting reports to protocol specifications. All standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs are standards. The RFC Editor receives submissions via electronic mail and conducts technical reviews appropriate to the document type.

Once assigned an RFC number and published, an RFC is never revised or re-issued with the same number. However, a protocol may be improved and re-documented many times across different RFCs. This memo serves as the authoritative reference for determining the correct current RFC for each protocol specification. The RFC states it is intended for quarterly distribution and notes the current version should not be used after 15 July 1996.
sections.eli5: RFCs are published documents about network ideas and rules. Once published, they never change, but a better version can be published with a new number. This list tells you which RFC has the current official version of each rule.
